paragraph_raw: During a strong earthquake, some of the worst damage is caused not by the shaking itself but by the ground beneath buildings. In loose, sandy soil that is soaked with water, the shaking pushes the grains closer together and raises the pressure of the water between them. For a short time the grains lose contact with one another, and the soil behaves like a thick liquid. Heavy buildings can then tilt, sink or even topple over while remaining largely undamaged. In 1964, apartment blocks in Niigata, Japan, famously tipped onto their sides. In Turkey's 1999 Marmara earthquake, many buildings in Adapazari sank into the ground or leaned dangerously. Engineers now test soil before construction and can strengthen it, for example by compacting it or draining the water.

paragraph_raw: Before vaccines, polio paralysed thousands of children every year, and in the worst cases it stopped the muscles used for breathing. paragraph_raw: In 1971, the psychologist Philip Zimbardo turned a basement at Stanford University into a mock prison. Twenty-four male students were randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners. More recently, however, recordings and interviews have revealed that guards were encouraged to be tough, and at least one prisoner later said he had exaggerated his breakdown. Many psychologists now treat its conclusions with caution.

paragraph_raw: Whooping cough, or pertussis, is a bacterial infection that starts like an ordinary cold. After a week or two, however, it causes violent coughing fits, often followed by a high-pitched 'whoop' as the patient struggles to breathe in. For this reason, many countries now offer the vaccine to pregnant women, whose antibodies cross the placenta and protect the baby in its first weeks.

paragraph_raw: For most of history, time was measured by the movement of the Earth, but our planet's spin is slightly irregular. Since 1967, the second has instead been defined by atoms: it is the time taken for a particular kind of radiation from caesium atoms to complete 9,192,631,770 cycles. Atomic clocks based on this principle would lose less than a second in millions of years. The newest optical clocks are so precise that they can detect the tiny difference in the flow of time between a shelf and the floor, because time passes slightly faster further from the Earth's gravity. Such clocks keep satellite navigation and financial networks synchronised.

paragraph_raw: When the heart's electrical rhythm suddenly becomes chaotic, it stops pumping blood effectively, and the person collapses. This is called cardiac arrest, and every minute without treatment sharply reduces the chance of survival. The most effective treatment is an electric shock from a defibrillator, which can reset the heart's rhythm. Public places such as airports and stadiums now often keep automated versions on their walls. These devices are designed for untrained people: they give spoken instructions and analyse the heart's rhythm themselves, delivering a shock only if it is needed. Used together with chest compressions, they can roughly double survival rates.

paragraph_raw: Radon is a radioactive gas produced naturally when uranium in soil and rocks breaks down. It has no colour, smell or taste, so people can be exposed for years without knowing. Outdoors it quickly spreads out and is harmless, but it can seep into buildings through cracks in floors and build up in basements and poorly ventilated rooms. Fortunately, testing a home is simple and cheap, and high levels can usually be reduced by sealing cracks and improving ventilation.

paragraph_raw: In 1957, the Sydney Opera House was expected to open in 1963 at a cost of seven million Australian dollars. It opened in 1973, having cost over one hundred million. Such overruns are so common that the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky gave the tendency a name: the planning fallacy. People estimate how long a task will take by imagining how it should go, rather than by remembering how similar tasks went. In one study, students predicted they would finish their theses in about a month, but on average took about 55 days. A useful remedy is to ask how long comparable projects actually took.

paragraph_raw: Imagine two suspects arrested for a crime and questioned in separate rooms. Each is offered a deal. If one betrays the other while the partner stays silent, the betrayer goes free and the partner gets ten years. If both stay silent, each gets only one year. If both betray, each gets five. Whatever the partner does, betraying seems the better choice for each individual, yet if both reason this way they end up worse off than if they had trusted each other. In 1980, the political scientist Robert Axelrod organised a tournament in which computer programs played this game against each other many times. paragraph_raw: Universal basic income is the idea that every adult should receive a regular payment from the state, with no conditions attached. Supporters argue it would reduce poverty, simplify welfare systems and protect workers as automation replaces some jobs. paragraph_raw: More than a century ago, the French engineer Max Ringelmann asked men to pull on a rope, alone and in groups. paragraph_raw: In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons noticed something puzzling. James Watt's improved steam engine used coal far more efficiently than earlier designs, so one might expect Britain to burn less coal. Instead, coal use soared. Because the engines were now cheaper to run, they became profitable in many more industries, and total demand grew. This effect, now called the Jevons paradox, still matters today. More efficient cars, lighting or computers can lower costs so much that people use them more, wiping out some or even all of the expected savings. For this reason, some experts argue that efficiency alone cannot be relied on to cut energy use.

paragraph_raw: In 1964, two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were troubled by a faint, steady hiss in their large horn-shaped antenna. paragraph_raw: Few diseases have carried as much fear and stigma as leprosy. paragraph_raw: The word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning forty days. In 1377, during repeated outbreaks of plague, the port city of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered that ships and travellers arriving from infected areas wait thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Venice later extended the period to forty days, and the longer term gave the practice its name. Why forty is unclear; it may have had religious significance, since forty days appears often in the Bible. Officials did not understand germs, but they had observed that disease seemed to arrive with people and goods. Later, cities built special isolation hospitals called lazarettos on islands near their ports. The same basic idea, separating people who may have been exposed until it is clear they are not ill, was used again during the COVID-19 pandemic.

paragraph_raw: After Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, plants, animals and diseases began moving between the Americas and the rest of the world on a scale never seen before. Historians call this the Columbian Exchange. From the Americas came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and cocoa; from Europe, Africa and Asia went wheat, sugar cane, horses and cattle. The effects were enormous. The potato, which grows well in poor soil, helped populations in northern Europe expand, while maize became a staple in parts of Africa. Turkish cuisine, too, would look very different without tomatoes and peppers. But the exchange also had a terrible side: diseases such as smallpox, to which Native Americans had no immunity, killed a huge share of the population.

paragraph_raw: When another driver cuts in front of us, we tend to conclude that they are rude or careless. When we do the same thing, we explain it by our situation: we were late, or we did not see them. Psychologists call this tendency the fundamental attribution error: we overestimate the role of personality in other people's behaviour and underestimate the role of circumstances. In a classic 1967 study, participants read essays praising or criticising Fidel Castro and were told that the writers had been assigned their position. paragraph_raw: In a famous 1999 experiment, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to watch a short video of students passing basketballs and to count the passes made by the team in white. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the middle of the scene, beat their chest and walked off, remaining on screen for several seconds. About half the viewers never noticed the gorilla, and many refused to believe it had been there until they watched again. The effect, called inattentional blindness, shows that we see far less than we think when our attention is focused elsewhere. It has serious implications, for example for drivers using phones, who may look directly at a cyclist without registering it.

paragraph_raw: In 2002, surgeons in Texas published a startling study on knee surgery for osteoarthritis, one of the most common operations at the time. Some patients received the real procedure, in which damaged tissue was cleaned out of the joint. Others received a fake operation: they were given anaesthetic and small cuts in the skin, but nothing was done inside the knee. Patients did not know which group they were in. Two years later, both groups reported the same improvement in pain and movement. Similar sham-surgery trials have since questioned other common operations. Critics argue that fake surgery raises ethical concerns, since patients face risks without any possible physical benefit, yet supporters say it is the only way to discover whether an operation really works.

paragraph_raw: In 1948, psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students a personality test and handed each of them a personal description. Most rated it as highly accurate. paragraph_raw: Imagine a coin toss: heads, you win some money; tails, you lose 100 dollars. How much would the prize have to be before you accepted? Most people demand around 200 dollars. paragraph_raw: In 1986, about 3.5 million people a year, mostly in Africa and Asia, suffered from Guinea worm disease. People swallowed the worm's larvae in tiny water fleas when they drank from ponds. About a year later, a worm up to a metre long slowly pushed its way out through a burning blister, usually on the leg. Seeking relief, victims often put the limb into water, where the worm released new larvae and the cycle began again. There is no vaccine and no medicine. Yet a campaign led by the Carter Center has reduced cases to fewer than twenty a year, using simple tools: cloth filters for drinking water, health education, and keeping patients away from water sources. If it succeeds, Guinea worm will be the first human disease eradicated without a vaccine or drug.

paragraph_raw: In 1935, the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz introduced an operation that cut connections in the front of the brain to treat severe mental illness. He reported that many patients became calmer, and in 1949 he received the Nobel Prize. In the United States, Walter Freeman developed a faster version, inserting an instrument through the eye socket, sometimes in under ten minutes and outside an operating room. Tens of thousands of Americans were lobotomised. Many patients were indeed calmer, but often because they had become passive and emotionally flat, and some never lived independently again. By the mid-1950s, the first effective psychiatric drugs offered an alternative, and the operation fell out of use. Today it is often cited as a warning about treatments adopted before their long-term effects are properly studied.

paragraph_raw: Imagine a radio station funded entirely by listeners' donations. Anyone can tune in, whether they pay or not. Each listener may reason that one small donation will make no difference, and that the station will survive anyway. If enough people think this way, it closes, and everyone loses something they valued. Economists call this the free rider problem. It appears whenever a benefit cannot easily be limited to those who pay for it, from street lighting to national defence, and even in group projects at school. Societies have developed several responses. Governments fund some services through compulsory taxes. Charities publish lists of donors or offer small gifts, and communities rely on social pressure, since few people like being seen as the one who did not contribute.

paragraph_raw: In the valley of the Orkhon River in present-day Mongolia stand stone monuments carved in the 730s for the Turkic ruler Bilge Kagan and his brother Kul Tigin. paragraph_raw: Red and green light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, were invented in the 1960s, but a bright blue one eluded scientists for three decades. paragraph_raw: Sharks are fish, dolphins are mammals, and the extinct ichthyosaurs were reptiles, yet all three evolved the same streamlined shape, with a pointed snout, a dorsal fin and a powerful tail. Biologists call this convergent evolution: unrelated species facing similar challenges arrive at similar solutions. The camera-like eye evolved separately in vertebrates and in octopuses. Interestingly, the octopus version is arguably better designed, because its nerve fibres run behind the light-sensitive cells rather than in front of them, so it has no blind spot. Convergence suggests that the laws of physics strongly limit the range of workable designs.

paragraph_raw: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, hat makers in Europe and America often used a mercury solution to turn animal fur into felt. Working in poorly ventilated rooms, they breathed in mercury vapour for years. Many developed trembling hands, memory loss, extreme shyness and sudden bursts of anger. In the hat-making town of Danbury, Connecticut, the tremors were so common that locals called them the 'Danbury shakes'. The expression 'mad as a hatter' probably reflects this poisoning, although scholars still argue about whether Lewis Carroll's famous character was based on it. The United States did not ban mercury in hat-making until 1941.

paragraph_raw: In a 1999 study, American psychologists gave men and women with strong maths backgrounds a difficult maths test. When participants were told that the test usually showed differences between men and women, the women scored noticeably lower than the men. When they were told that it showed no such differences, the gap disappeared. Psychologists Claude Steele and his colleagues called this stereotype threat: the worry of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group can itself harm performance, perhaps by using up mental energy needed for the task. Later studies suggest the effect may be smaller than first thought, but it remains widely discussed in education.

paragraph_raw: In 1950, during a lunchtime conversation about flying saucers, the physicist Enrico Fermi suddenly asked his colleagues, 'But where is everybody?' His reasoning was simple. paragraph_raw: Between 1856 and 1863, Gregor Mendel, a monk in the city of Brno, grew and studied about 28,000 pea plants in his monastery garden. He chose peas because they have clear, either-or features, such as purple or white flowers and smooth or wrinkled seeds. When he crossed purple-flowered plants with white-flowered ones, all the offspring had purple flowers. Yet when those offspring were bred together, white flowers reappeared in roughly one plant in four. Mendel concluded that each plant carries two units for every trait, one from each parent, and that one unit can hide the other without destroying it. He published his results in 1866, but they were largely ignored. Only in 1900 did three scientists, working separately, rediscover his paper and recognise it as the foundation of genetics.

paragraph_raw: Asbestos is a natural mineral made of tiny fibres. Because it does not burn and insulates well, it was used throughout the twentieth century in roofs, pipes, walls and car brakes, and was often praised as a 'magic mineral'. Its danger lies in the fibres. When asbestos is broken or worn, they float into the air, and if breathed in they can lodge in the lungs for life. Diseases such as mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining around the lungs, may appear twenty to fifty years after exposure, which helped delay action against the material. Many countries have now banned it; Turkey did so in 2010. However, it remains inside many older buildings, where it is mostly harmless unless disturbed. paragraph_raw: For centuries, sailors could work out how far north or south they were from the height of the Sun, but not how far east or west. paragraph_raw: In 1836, Michael Faraday lined a room with metal foil and charged it with powerful electricity. Inside, his instruments detected no electric effect. When charge builds up on a closed metal shell, it spreads over the outer surface in a way that cancels the electric field inside. Such a shell is now called a Faraday cage, and it does not even need to be solid: a mesh works, provided its holes are much smaller than the waves it must block. This also explains why a car offers good protection from lightning: the current flows around the metal body, not, as many people believe, because the rubber tyres insulate it.

paragraph_raw: A panic attack is a sudden wave of intense fear that usually peaks within ten minutes. In 1839, according to his own account, a mixture of rubber and sulphur accidentally touched a hot stove. Instead of melting, it charred like leather and stayed flexible. This process, later called vulcanisation, made rubber useful for everything from boots to tyres. Yet Goodyear died in debt in 1860, and the famous tyre company bearing his name was founded decades later with no link to his family.

paragraph_raw: Norovirus, often called the winter vomiting bug, causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea that usually last one to three days. It is one of the most contagious viruses known: a tiny number of particles can be enough to make someone ill, and an infected person releases billions. The virus can survive for days on door handles, railings and taps, which explains why outbreaks spread so quickly on cruise ships, in hospitals and in schools. Alcohol-based hand gels work poorly against it, so health officials recommend washing with soap and water and cleaning surfaces with bleach. Most healthy adults recover fully, but young children and older people can become dangerously dehydrated.

paragraph_raw: Many people assume that the main danger of falling into cold water is hypothermia, the dangerous cooling of the body. In fact, in the first minute, the bigger threat is cold water shock. The sudden cold triggers an uncontrollable gasp, followed by rapid breathing, and a person who goes under at that moment can inhale water. Swimming is also much harder than usual. Hypothermia, by contrast, usually takes thirty minutes or more to develop. Safety organisations therefore advise anyone who falls in to resist the urge to swim hard, lie back and float until their breathing settles, and only then make a plan to get out or call for help.

paragraph_raw: In a 1998 experiment, a researcher stopped people on a university campus to ask for directions. While they were talking, two men carrying a large door walked rudely between them. In the few seconds the view was blocked, the researcher was replaced by another man with a different height, clothing and voice, who continued the conversation. About half of the people giving directions never noticed the switch. This phenomenon, called change blindness, shows that we store far less visual detail than we believe. Our sense of seeing a rich, complete scene is partly an illusion, which matters for eyewitness testimony and for drivers who glance away from the road.

paragraph_raw: In 1772, the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange showed that in a system of two large bodies, such as the Sun and the Earth, there are five special points where a small object can stay in the same position relative to both. At these points, the gravitational pulls of the two bodies and the motion of the orbit balance out. A point about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth towards the Sun offers an uninterrupted view of the Sun, and solar observatories are parked there. The equivalent point on the far side of Earth, where the Sun, Earth and Moon all lie in one direction so a single shield can block their heat, is home to the James Webb Space Telescope. Two other points, ahead of and behind a planet in its orbit, are stable enough to collect natural objects: thousands of asteroids gather at those of Jupiter.

paragraph_raw: Early electronic computers relied on vacuum tubes, glass bulbs that acted as switches. They were large, consumed a great deal of power, gave off heat and frequently burned out; the ENIAC computer of 1945 contained about 17,500 of them. In December 1947, three researchers at Bell Laboratories in the United States, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley, demonstrated a tiny device that could do the same job: the transistor. It was smaller, cooler and far more reliable, and the three men shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Within a decade, transistors had made pocket radios possible. Shockley later founded his own company in California, but his difficult management style drove eight of his best employees to leave and start a rival firm, an event often seen as the birth of Silicon Valley. Today a single smartphone chip contains billions of transistors.

paragraph_raw: For decades, patients were told to finish every course of antibiotics, even after feeling better, to avoid creating resistant bacteria. In 2017, however, a group of British experts argued in a leading medical journal that this advice had little evidence behind it. Resistance, they explained, often develops in the harmless bacteria living in our gut and on our skin, and the longer these bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, the more chances they have to adapt. Taking drugs for longer than necessary might therefore increase resistance rather than prevent it. Trials have since shown that, for several common infections, shorter courses work just as well. The experts were careful to add that some diseases, such as tuberculosis, do need long treatment, and that patients should not simply stop on their own, but should ask their doctor about the right length of treatment.

paragraph_raw: The Book of Dede Korkut is a collection of twelve stories from the Oghuz Turks, a people who lived in Central Asia and later moved into Anatolia and Azerbaijan. The tales were passed down orally for centuries before being written down, probably in the fifteenth or sixteenth century. For a long time, only two manuscripts were known, one in Dresden and one in the Vatican. In most stories, the wise old bard Dede Korkut appears to give heroes their names, offer advice and close the tale with a blessing. The stories describe brave warriors, but also strong women who ride, shoot arrows and fight alongside men. One tale features Tepegoz, a one-eyed giant whose defeat closely resembles that of the Cyclops in Homer's Odyssey, a parallel that still fascinates scholars. In 2018, the heritage of Dede Korkut was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

paragraph_raw: Old chocolate sometimes develops a white or grey coating, which many people mistake for mould. It is usually one of two kinds of bloom. paragraph_raw: In 1970, the psychologist Gordon Gallup put a red mark on the faces of anaesthetised chimpanzees. When they woke and looked in a mirror, they touched the mark on their own faces, suggesting they understood that the reflection was themselves. This mirror test has since been passed by orangutans, dolphins, an Asian elephant and magpies. In 2019, researchers reported that a fish, the cleaner wrasse, also seemed to pass, scraping the mark against the tank floor. Some scientists concluded that the test is less demanding than thought; others argued that fish might be smarter than we assume. paragraph_raw: Cystic echinococcosis, also known as hydatid disease, is caused by a tapeworm that lives in the intestines of dogs. Its eggs pass out in the dog's faeces and can contaminate soil, water and vegetables. paragraph_raw: In a classic 1973 study, researchers chose preschool children who already enjoyed drawing. paragraph_raw: Since it was first seen in 1996, a strange disease has killed most of the Tasmanian devils living in the wild. paragraph_raw: Before the 1790s, soldiers wounded in battle often lay where they fell until the fighting was over, sometimes for a day or more, and many died who could have been saved. This method of sorting patients became known as triage, from a French word meaning 'to sort'. paragraph_raw: In 1577, the astronomer Taqi al-Din, known in Turkish as Takiyuddin, completed one of the most advanced observatories of its time in Istanbul, with the support of Sultan Murad III. paragraph_raw: In 1954, the Turkish-born psychologist Muzafer Sherif took twenty-two eleven-year-old boys to a summer camp in Oklahoma. The boys were split into two groups, which at first did not know about each other. When the groups were brought together for a series of competitions, such as tug-of-war and baseball, hostility quickly grew: they called each other names, burned each other's flag and raided each other's cabins. What worked was giving them goals that neither group could achieve alone, such as repairing the camp's water supply or pulling a broken-down truck. After several such tasks, friendships formed across group lines. Sherif concluded that conflict often grows out of competition for limited rewards, and cooperation on shared goals can reduce it.

paragraph_raw: In a famous 1978 study, psychologists interviewed recent lottery winners and found that, after some time had passed, they were not much happier than people who had won nothing. They also took less pleasure in everyday activities such as chatting with friends. This tendency to adapt to good fortune, returning to roughly our usual level of happiness, is called the hedonic treadmill: we keep running towards the next reward, yet stay in the same place. Later research showed that adaptation is not always complete; long-term unemployment, for example, can lower happiness for years. Still, the idea helps explain why a new car or phone thrills us only briefly.

paragraph_raw: Carbon capture aims to stop carbon dioxide from reaching the atmosphere, or to remove it once it is there. Some systems trap the gas from the chimneys of power plants and factories; others, called direct air capture, pull it straight out of ordinary air. The captured gas can be pumped deep underground. Since 1996, a Norwegian gas field has stored about a million tonnes a year beneath the North Sea, and in Iceland, carbon dioxide dissolved in water is injected into volcanic rock, where it turns to stone within two years. Yet the scale is tiny compared with the more than 35 billion tonnes humans release each year, and the technology is expensive and uses a lot of energy. Supporters see it as essential for industries that are hard to clean up; critics fear it gives polluters an excuse to delay cutting emissions.

paragraph_raw: The oldest known pieces of Earth are not great slabs of rock but tiny crystals of a mineral called zircon, some no wider than a human hair. Found in the Jack Hills of Western Australia, the oldest have been dated to about 4.4 billion years ago, only around 150 million years after our planet formed. Zircon is ideal for this work. paragraph_raw: On Earth, every step we take puts weight on our bones, and that stress keeps them strong. In the weightlessness of space, the stress disappears, and astronauts can lose 1 to 1.5 per cent of the bone mass in their hips and spine every month, roughly what an older person with osteoporosis might lose in a year. paragraph_raw: In 1751, the French writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean d'Alembert published the first volume of the Encyclopedie, an enormous project that aimed to gather all human knowledge. paragraph_raw: In the early twentieth century, people in the American South were often described by outsiders as lazy and slow. paragraph_raw: In a famous 1961 experiment, the psychologist Albert Bandura showed young children an adult playing with a large inflatable doll called Bobo. For some children, the adult attacked the doll, hitting it with a mallet, kicking it and shouting phrases such as 'Sock him in the nose!' Others saw an adult who played quietly. Later, each child was left alone in a room with toys, including a Bobo doll. Children who had watched the aggressive adult were far more likely to attack the doll, often copying the exact actions and words. Bandura argued that children learn not only through rewards and punishments, but also simply by watching others. Critics have pointed out that Bobo is designed to be punched and bounce back, so hitting it may be play rather than true aggression, but the study remains central to debates about violent media.

paragraph_raw: Hasankeyf, an ancient town on the River Tigris in south-eastern Turkey, had been inhabited for thousands of years. paragraph_raw: After the horrors of the Second World War, the newly founded United Nations set out to define rights that every person should have, regardless of nationality, religion or wealth. A committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, the widow of the American president, brought together experts from countries including China, France and Lebanon, who often disagreed about the philosophical basis of rights. On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with 48 countries in favour, none against and eight abstaining. The declaration was not a legally binding treaty, but it inspired many later agreements and national constitutions. It has been translated into more than 500 languages, more than any other document, and 10 December is now celebrated each year as Human Rights Day.

paragraph_raw: Where did the Moon come from? For centuries, nobody had a convincing answer. When the Apollo astronauts brought back rock samples, scientists found that lunar rocks were remarkably similar to those of Earth's mantle, but contained relatively little water or iron. The leading explanation since the 1980s is the giant-impact hypothesis. About 4.5 billion years ago, it suggests, a body roughly the size of Mars, later named Theia, struck the young Earth a glancing blow. The collision melted and vaporised vast amounts of rock, throwing debris into orbit, where it gradually gathered into the Moon. The theory explains a great deal, but not everything: computer models predict that most of the Moon should come from Theia, yet its rocks are almost chemically identical to Earth's. Some researchers now suggest the impact was even more violent, mixing the two bodies thoroughly.

paragraph_raw: In 2015, a team of 270 researchers tried to repeat 100 psychology experiments that had been published in leading journals. Although almost all the original studies had reported significant results, only about a third of the repeat attempts did. The project helped spark what became known as the replication crisis. Part of the problem lay in how research was rewarded: journals preferred surprising, positive findings, so studies that found nothing often went unpublished, and researchers could try many analyses until one produced an eye-catching result. Psychology was not alone; similar problems were found in medicine and economics. In response, many scientists now publicly register their plans before collecting data and share their raw data, so others can check their work. Some famous findings have not survived, but supporters argue that science is doing exactly what it should: correcting itself.

paragraph_raw: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in the largest volcanic explosion in recorded history, killing tens of thousands of people nearby. paragraph_raw: Contact tracing is one of the oldest tools in public health. When someone is diagnosed with an infectious disease, trained workers ask whom they have been close to, then find those people, warn them and, if needed, test or isolate them. paragraph_raw: In 1974, the economist Richard Easterlin noticed something puzzling. Within a country, richer people reported being happier than poorer ones. paragraph_raw: When enough people in a community are immune to an infectious disease, either through vaccination or past infection, the disease struggles to spread, because each infected person meets too few people who can catch it. This indirect protection, called herd immunity, shields those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies and people with weak immune systems. The share of people who need to be immune depends on how contagious the disease is. For measles, one of the most contagious diseases known, it is about 95 per cent; for polio, roughly 80 per cent. This is why even a small fall in vaccination rates can allow measles outbreaks to return, while seeming to make little difference for other diseases. Relying on natural infection to reach herd immunity, meanwhile, would cost many lives along the way.

paragraph_raw: In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve countries, including both the United States and the Soviet Union, signed a treaty about the one continent with no native population: Antarctica. paragraph_raw: In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley, appeared to be biased against women: 44 per cent of men who applied to its graduate programmes were admitted, compared with 35 per cent of women. Yet when researchers examined each department separately, most admitted women at similar or even higher rates than men. The explanation was that women had mostly applied to highly competitive departments, which rejected most applicants of either sex, while men had applied more to departments with lots of places. paragraph_raw: During the Second World War, the German military encrypted its messages with Enigma machines, which scrambled each letter through a series of rotating wheels. The settings changed every day, giving around 158 million million million possible combinations, so the Germans believed the code was unbreakable. The first breakthrough, however, came from Polish mathematicians, including Marian Rejewski, who reconstructed the machine in the early 1930s and shared their work with Britain and France shortly before the war. At Bletchley Park in England, Alan Turing and others built electromechanical machines called 'bombes' to test possible settings quickly. They exploited German habits, such as starting messages with predictable phrases like weather reports. Historians estimate that the intelligence gained may have shortened the war by up to two years, though such figures are hard to prove.

paragraph_raw: Almost everyone sleeps badly sometimes, but for about one adult in ten, insomnia becomes a long-term problem, lasting for months. Many reach for sleeping pills, which can help for a short time but often lose their effect and may cause drowsiness the next day. Medical guidelines in many countries now recommend a different first treatment: cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I. Surprisingly, one of its key techniques is to spend less time in bed. Patients go to bed only when sleepy and get up at the same time every day, even after a bad night, so that the pressure to sleep builds up. They also learn to leave the bedroom if they lie awake, so the bed becomes linked with sleep rather than worry. The first weeks can be tiring, but the improvements tend to last far longer than those from pills.

paragraph_raw: Stuttering, in which the flow of speech is broken by repeated sounds, stretched sounds or silent blocks, affects around one per cent of adults and many more young children, most of whom grow out of it. For centuries it was blamed on nervousness, bad parenting or even the shape of the tongue, and some nineteenth-century surgeons cut patients' tongue muscles in an attempt to cure it. Research now shows that stuttering has strong genetic and neurological roots; brain scans reveal differences in the areas that plan and time speech. Anxiety does not cause stuttering, though it can make it worse. Many people who stutter speak fluently when singing or talking in unison with others, which suggests the problem lies in starting and timing speech rather than in knowing what to say. Speech therapy can help, and many famous actors, politicians and writers have stuttered.

paragraph_raw: In the 1920s, many astronomers believed that the universe was static and that our Milky Way might be all there was. Then, in 1924, Edwin Hubble used the new telescope on Mount Wilson in California to show that some fuzzy patches of light, then called nebulae, were in fact separate galaxies, far beyond our own. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre had already predicted this in 1927, arguing that the universe was expanding. If everything is flying apart, then in the distant past everything must have been packed together, an idea that grew into the Big Bang theory. Einstein, who had added a term to his equations to keep the universe still, later reportedly called it his biggest blunder.

paragraph_raw: Between 1346 and 1353, a pandemic of plague swept across Asia, the Middle East and Europe, killing perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population. paragraph_raw: Chemotherapy has an unexpected origin. During both world wars, doctors noticed that soldiers exposed to mustard gas had very low numbers of white blood cells. In the early 1940s, the pharmacologists Louis Goodman and Alfred Gilman at Yale wondered whether a related chemical could attack cancers of the white blood cells. In 1942, they treated a patient with advanced lymphoma, and his tumours shrank dramatically, though the cancer later returned. The work was kept secret during the war and published in 1946. It offered early proof that a drug could shrink a cancer, and it opened the way for the many chemotherapy drugs used today.

paragraph_raw: The polygraph, often called a lie detector, was developed in the early 1920s. It records changes in breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and sweating while a person answers questions, on the assumption that lying causes stress. paragraph_raw: Every second, around 60 billion tiny particles called neutrinos pass through each square centimetre of your body, most of them produced by nuclear reactions in the Sun. You feel nothing, because neutrinos have almost no mass and no electric charge, and they hardly ever interact with matter; many could pass through a light-year of solid lead without stopping. Their existence was proposed in 1930 by Wolfgang Pauli to explain missing energy in radioactive decay, but they were not detected until 1956. To catch the rare collisions, scientists build huge detectors deep underground, shielded from other radiation. One, IceCube, uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. Studying neutrinos helps scientists look deep inside the Sun and exploding stars, places from which light cannot escape directly.

paragraph_raw: When AIDS was first identified in 1981, a diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. The virus that causes it, HIV, attacks the immune system, leaving the body unable to fight infections. Then, in 1996, doctors began combining several antiretroviral drugs at once. Because the virus mutates quickly, it could resist one drug, but rarely three together. Deaths in wealthy countries fell dramatically within a few years. Today, a person diagnosed early and treated consistently can expect a nearly normal lifespan. Just as importantly, studies have shown that when treatment reduces the virus in the blood to undetectable levels, it cannot be passed on through sex, a finding summarised as 'undetectable equals untransmittable'. The main challenges now are reaching everyone who needs testing and treatment, and the stigma that still stops many people from seeking help.

paragraph_raw: Erythropoietin, or EPO, is a hormone made by the kidneys that tells the body to produce more red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles. A synthetic version was developed in the 1980s to treat anaemia in patients with kidney disease, and it transformed their lives. But endurance athletes, especially cyclists, soon realised that extra red blood cells could greatly improve their performance. Because natural EPO is always present in the blood, the artificial version was very difficult to detect, and its use spread widely in the 1990s. It was also dangerous: thickened blood can cause clots, heart attacks and strokes, especially during sleep. A urine test was introduced in 2000, and later the 'biological passport', which tracks an athlete's blood over time, made cheating far harder, though not impossible.

paragraph_raw: Why does rubbing a bumped knee make it hurt less? In 1965, the scientists Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed an answer known as the gate control theory. The theory also helped explain why emotions and attention affect pain, since the brain can send signals down to the gate. paragraph_raw: Every few years, the trade winds that normally blow westward across the tropical Pacific weaken, and warm water spreads east towards South America. paragraph_raw: Unlike the vaccines for measles or polio, which protect for many years, the flu vaccine has to be updated and taken again every year. The reason is that influenza viruses change constantly. Mutations in the proteins on their surface allow them to slip past the immunity people built up from earlier infections or vaccines. Twice a year, experts working with the World Health Organization study samples collected around the world and predict which strains are most likely to spread in the coming season, one for each hemisphere. Because vaccines take months to produce, the choice must be made early, and when the prediction is wrong, the vaccine works less well.

paragraph_raw: Paper money first appeared in China. Around the tenth century, merchants in Sichuan who did not want to carry heavy strings of iron coins began leaving them with trusted dealers in exchange for written receipts, which could be traded. When Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the late thirteenth century, many Europeans found it hard to believe. paragraph_raw: The Caesarean section, in which a baby is delivered through a cut in the mother's abdomen, is now one of the most common operations in the world. paragraph_raw: According to Chinese records, in the year 105, a court official named Cai Lun presented the emperor with a new writing material made from tree bark, old rags, hemp and fishing nets, pounded into pulp, spread thin and dried. Archaeologists have since found older pieces of paper, so Cai Lun probably improved and promoted the process rather than inventing it, but his recipe made paper cheap and practical. Before that, the Chinese wrote on bamboo strips, which were heavy, or silk, which was expensive. The secret of papermaking spread slowly westward. Tradition says that after a battle in 751, Chinese prisoners taught it to craftsmen in Samarkand, and from there it reached Baghdad, then Europe, where it later made the printing revolution possible.

paragraph_raw: For many cities and natural sites, tourism is both a blessing and a curse. It brings jobs and income, but too many visitors can overwhelm places that were never designed for them. In Venice, around twenty million visitors a year crowd into a historic centre where fewer than fifty thousand residents remain, and in 2024 the city began charging day-trippers an entry fee on busy days. Barcelona has limited new hotels and tourist flats, as rising rents push locals out. In Turkey, visitors at Pamukkale must walk barefoot on set paths to protect the white terraces. The challenge is to share the benefits of tourism without destroying the very things that attract people in the first place.

paragraph_raw: In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist working at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva, wrote a proposal for sharing information between researchers. His manager reportedly scribbled on it, 'Vague but exciting'. Berners-Lee went on to create the three basic tools of the World Wide Web: a language for writing pages, a system of web addresses, and rules for sending pages between computers. He also built the first web browser and the first website, which was opened to the public in 1991. The internet itself already existed, linking computers since the 1960s and 70s; the web was a way of using it. Crucially, CERN agreed in 1993 to make the technology free for anyone, without patents or fees, which allowed it to spread across the world within a few years.

paragraph_raw: Vecihi Hurkus was a pilot in the Ottoman army during the First World War and later in the Turkish War of Independence. In 1925, with very limited means, he designed and built a small aircraft in a workshop in Izmir. Named Vecihi K-VI, it is considered the first aircraft designed and built in Turkey, and he flew it himself, although he had not received official permission and was later fined. In the 1930s he built further aircraft and opened a civil flying school in Istanbul, where many young people took their first flying lessons. His career was full of setbacks, from bureaucratic obstacles to a shortage of money, but his determination made him a symbol of Turkish aviation, and his life later became the subject of books and a film.

paragraph_raw: People often say 'I'm so OCD' when they mean they like a tidy desk, but obsessive-compulsive disorder is far more serious. It affects around one to two per cent of people and involves two linked parts. Obsessions are unwanted, distressing thoughts that keep returning, such as fears of contamination or of causing harm. Compulsions are repeated actions, like washing hands or checking locks, performed to reduce the anxiety. The relief is only temporary, so the cycle repeats and can take up hours each day. Most people with OCD know their fears are unrealistic, which makes the condition especially frustrating. The most effective treatment is a form of therapy called exposure and response prevention, in which patients gradually face their fears without performing the compulsion, sometimes combined with medication.

topic: Sport (Pierre de Coubertin and the Modern Olympics)
paragraph_raw: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece for over a thousand years before ending in the late fourth century. In the 1880s, a French aristocrat, Pierre de Coubertin, became convinced that sport could build character and bring nations together, and he campaigned to revive the Games. In 1894 he founded the International Olympic Committee in Paris, and two years later the first modern Olympics were held in Athens, with around 240 athletes from fourteen countries, all of them men. Coubertin wanted the Games to move between cities, and he designed the five interlocking rings in 1913, representing the continents that would take part. Yet he opposed women competing, calling it 'impractical, uninteresting' and improper. Today, women make up about half of all Olympic athletes.

paragraph_raw: Basque, spoken by around 750,000 people in northern Spain and south-western France, is a linguistic puzzle. Most languages in Europe belong to the Indo-European family, which includes English, Spanish, Russian and Hindi, but Basque is related to no other living language. Many linguists think it is a survivor from before the Indo-European languages arrived in Europe several thousand years ago. Its grammar is very different from its neighbours: verbs change to show both the subject and the object, and a special ending marks who performed an action. Under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, from 1939 to 1975, public use of Basque was severely restricted. Since then, schools teaching in Basque have helped the number of speakers grow, an unusual success story for a minority language.
